κυρίῳ κληθεὶς δοῦλος ἀπελεύθερος κυρίου ἐστίν· οἷον· Ἐκλήθης δοῦλος; τοῦτο ἴσθι
ὅτι οὐ μόνον οὐκ εἶ δοῦλος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔχεις τι ἐλευθερίας διὰ τὸν κύριον. ὁ γὰρ
ἀπελεύθερος οὔτε καθαρῶς ἐλεύθερός ἐστιν οὐδὲ ἔτι δοῦλος, ὡς εἶναι τὸν μὲν
καθαρὸν πάντῃ ἐλεύθερον τὸν δὲ ἐν γάμῳ δοῦλον· ὅταν δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ ᾖ δοῦλος, τότε
λέγομεν ὅτι ἀπελεύθερος κυρίου ἐστίν. ὁ δὲ ἐλεύθερος κληθεὶς δοῦλός ἐστιν οὐ
γυναικός, ἀλλὰ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ θεοῦ. Τιμῆς ἠγοράσθητε· μὴ γίνεσθε δοῦλοι

pass_a_gloss: called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman—meaning: called as a slave? Realize you are not merely no longer a slave; through the Lord you already hold a share of freedom. A freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, so the wholly pure person is free and the married person a slave; yet when slavery is “in the Lord,” we call him the Lord’s freedman. The person called free is enslaved not to a wife but to God’s Word. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of people. Grasp with all strength the Word who bought us out; let us make peace by the blood poured for us. Earlier, on unmarried and married, we noted he tightens then loosens. He does the same here with “do not become slaves of people,” sharpening the word and urging those who can to live purely, each in the calling where he was called. Note that other interpreters take foreskin and circumcision by the letter; they say he often leaves the present theme for other statutes fitting each group. On virgins I lack a Lord’s precept, yet I offer a judgment as one the Lord has shown mercy to make trustworthy. Some commands are required; others are not required but left free and handed to choice by God. Those without which salvation fails are the required ones; greater acts than the required—acts we may omit and still be saved—are not God’s precept. Hear Jesus’ gospel: when you have done all commanded, you should say we are useless servants; we did what we owed. If doing all commanded still leaves me a useless servant, when do I escape that label? When ambition climbs past the commanded: if I keep “do not commit adultery” and refuse a lustful look, I did what I owed. If I stay virgin without order or precept, I no longer say over that success “we are useless servants; we did what we owed.” So with the rest: if I neither steal nor overreach, we should say we are useless servants. If I sell all I own and give to the poor, I no longer say I am useless; I did what I owed. Hence Paul: on virgins I lack a Lord’s precept, yet I offer a judgment as one the Lord has shown mercy to make trustworthy. When the Lord tells disciples not all receive the word but those to whom it is given, and adds “let the one able receive it,” he did not command; he left freedom. So I offer a judgment, Paul says, and to show the Lord speaks in him he adds “as one shown mercy by the Lord to be trustworthy.” I judge this fine because of the present necessity—that a person be thus. “Necessity” means dwelling in the body, as elsewhere “remaining in the flesh is more necessary for you.” Four times here Paul names “good”: first, good not to touch a woman; second, good if they remain as I; third, I judge this good because of present necessity; fourth, good for a person to be thus. Notice how chastity talk is paired with “good,” while marriage talk is paired with “the one who marries does not sin.” Bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Across the whole argument he tightens and loosens so the hearer, using his own power, may judge what he can and which discipline he can take. Here too he turns away from dissolving marriage, then again urges purity. So he called the married husband “bound”; and if binding is a hard spot, flee hard spots as far as you can. Bound to a wife? Do not seek release; unbound, guard yourself lest you be bound—for you will find them tied by marital desire. The person already caught in marriage must not chase untimely freedom but stay in that slavery; and if released, must not seek a wife. If you marry, he says, you have not sinned. He did not say “if you marry, it is good,” but “if you marry, you have not sinned”—keep that gap. And
pass_b_english: called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; as if: Were you called a slave? Know this, that you are not only not a slave, but you also have something of freedom because of the Lord. For the freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, so that the one wholly pure is free and the one in marriage a slave; but when he is a slave in the Lord, then we say he is the Lord's freedman. And the one called free is a slave not of a wife but of the Word of God. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. With all your strength understand the one who bought us out, the Word of God; let us propitiate the blood poured out for us. We were saying in the word about unmarried and married that he tightens and loosens the word. So also here he has done, saying: Do not become slaves of human beings; for he as it were tightens and makes the word sharper, exhorting those able, as far as possible, to live purely, and each to live purely in the calling in which he was called. And one must know that the other interpreters have given the sense about uncircumcision and circumcision according to the letter; for customarily, they say, he passes from what is before him to other things, legislating for all what is fitting.

Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy (1 Corinthians 7:25). Of the commandments some are commanded, and some are not commanded but left free and entrusted to choice by God. For those without which one cannot be saved—these are the ones commanded; but the greater ones than the commanded, which even if we do not do we are saved, are not a command of God. Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. But if I remain a virgin, not ordered and not commanded, I no longer say over the achievement of virginity: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought. So also on the remaining commandments: if I do not steal or overreach, we ought to say we are unprofitable servants. But if I sell all that I have and give to the poor, I no longer say I am unprofitable; I have done what I ought. Therefore the apostle says: Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy. For in the Lord's saying to the disciples not all receive the word but those to whom it has been given, and he adds: let the one who is able to receive it receive it (Matthew 19:11–12); he did not command, but left it free. So I give an opinion, says the apostle, and to show that the Lord speaks in him he said as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.

I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity, that it is good for a person to be thus (1 Corinthians 7:26). By necessity he means the sojourn in the body, as also elsewhere he says: but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:24). Four times in the place the apostle named the good; for he says first: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; second: it is good for them if they remain as I also am; third: I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity; fourth: it is good for a person to be thus. You see how many things said about chastity are named with the good; but whatever is said about marriage, with the marrying person's not sinning.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be loosed. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife (1 Corinthians 7:27). Through the whole discourse, as has been said, he tightens and loosens, that the hearer, taking it in his own authority, may judge what he is able and to what exercise he can give himself. So also here he turned away from loosing marriage, and again exhorts to live purely. Therefore he called the married husband bound; and if to be bound is a circumstance, one must flee circumstances as far as possible. And do not seek to loose being bound to a wife; and the one not bound ought to guard himself lest he be bound; for truly you will find them bound by the marital love-charm. It is not permitted, then, for the one forestalled in marriage to seek untimely freedom, but to remain in the slavery; and if someone has been loosed, not to seek a wife. But if you also marry, he says, you have not sinned. He did not say: If you marry, it is good; but: If you marry, you have not sinned; keep the difference. And
